items.stem: Which of the following best describes "equality of outcome"?
options: A critical term for low-effort online support, such as liking or sharing, that may substitute for more demanding political action
John Rawls’s principle that social and economic inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society
A movement founded in 2013 by Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors and Opal Tometi to campaign against racism and police violence against Black people, which grew into a global protest wave in 2020
The principle that resources, income or results should be distributed more equally, often through redistribution by the state
items.answer: The principle that resources, income or results should be distributed more equally, often through redistribution by the state
items.markingKey: D. "equality of outcome" is the principle that resources, income or results should be distributed more equally, often through redistribution by the state.

items.stem: Explain the difference between substantive equality and formal equality.
items.answer: Formal equality means treating everyone the same in law; substantive equality takes account of different circumstances and may require positive measures to achieve equal results.
items.markingKey: Formal equality means treating everyone the same in law; substantive equality takes account of different circumstances and may require positive measures to achieve equal results. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why equality is an essentially contested concept.
items.answer: People disagree about what should be equal – rights, opportunities, resources or outcomes – and about how far equality should be balanced against liberty, merit and cultural values, so ideologies define it differently. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: People disagree about what should be equal – rights, opportunities, resources or outcomes – and about how far equality should be balanced against liberty, merit and cultural values, so ideologies define it differently. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Black women cannot be treated as only Black or only women; their experience is greater than the sum of racism and sexism; analysis without intersectionality cannot address their subordination

items.stem: "Equality of opportunity is impossible without some equality of outcome." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Significant inequality of outcome undermines equal opportunity, so some redistribution is necessary for fair chances.

items.stem: Which UN treaty, adopted in 1979, is often described as an international bill of rights for women?
options: CEDAW
The Istanbul Convention
The ICCPR
The Beijing Platform for Action
items.answer: CEDAW
items.markingKey: A. The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women has 189 parties.

items.stem: A student claims: "If laws treat everyone the same, equality has been achieved." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Formal legal equality can coexist with large differences in income, power and opportunity; substantive equality may require positive action.
items.markingKey: Formal legal equality can coexist with large differences in income, power and opportunity; substantive equality may require positive action. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the gender pay gap in the European Union shows gender inequality despite legal equality.
items.answer: Women in the EU earned on average about 12–13 per cent less per hour than men in the early 2020s; the EU Pay Transparency Directive (2023) requires firms to report and address pay gaps. Equal pay has been law since the Treaty of Rome (1957), but the persistent gap shows how structural factors sustain inequality.
items.markingKey: Context (Women in the EU earned on average about 12–13 per cent less per hour than men in the early 2020s; the EU Pay Transparency Directive (2023) requires firms to report and address pay gaps.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: Both undermine democracy; economic inequality distorts influence, while gender inequality limits who participates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wealth buys political influence; inequality erodes trust (Chile 2019); populism and polarisation. items.stem: Who founded the “Me Too” movement in 2006?
items.answer: Tarana Burke
items.markingKey: Tarana Burke. The hashtag went viral in 2017 after allegations against film producer Harvey Weinstein.

items.answer: It spread to many countries, with local versions such as #BalanceTonPorc in France, #MeTooIndia (2018) and #MiPrimerAcoso in Mexico.

items.stem: Distinguish between liberal feminism and radical feminism.
items.answer: Liberal feminism seeks equal rights and opportunities through legal and political reform within existing institutions; radical feminism argues that patriarchy is embedded in social structures and requires deeper transformation.

items.stem:
Source D
Movements organised through social media can mobilise millions within days, yet the success rate of mass non-violent campaigns has fallen. Digital visibility does not automatically lead to policy change; that depends on building organisation and coalitions, winning allies inside institutions and sustaining pressure over time.
— Erica Chenoweth, “The Future of Nonviolent Resistance”, Journal of Democracy (2020) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain how the source helps to evaluate the effectiveness of equality movements. [3]
items.answer: It suggests that success should be judged by institutional outcomes, not only by mobilisation; movements that build coalitions and sustain pressure are more likely to achieve change.
items.markingKey: It suggests that success should be judged by institutional outcomes, not only by mobilisation; movements that build coalitions and sustain pressure are more likely to achieve change. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Green Wave in Argentina (2018–2020), explain how it illustrates social movements and legislative change.
items.answer: Feminist movements, wearing green scarves, mobilised mass protests for legal abortion; after a defeat in the Senate in 2018, Congress legalised abortion in December 2020. Sustained mass mobilisation, building on Ni Una Menos, shifted public opinion and party positions, leading to legal change.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Movements for equality are more successful in democracies than in authoritarian states."

Black Lives Matter

items.stem: Distinguish between legislated candidate quotas and reserved seats.
items.answer: Reserved seats guarantee that a share of seats is held by women or another group (Rwanda, India); candidate quotas require parties to nominate a share of women but do not guarantee their election (Argentina, France).
items.markingKey: Reserved seats guarantee that a share of seats is held by women or another group (Rwanda, India); candidate quotas require parties to nominate a share of women but do not guarantee their election (Argentina, France). items.stem: Explain why composite indices of inequality are useful but limited.
items.answer: They summarise several dimensions in one comparable number, but depend on data quality and weighting choices, and national averages can hide inequality between regions, classes and ethnic groups.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They summarise several dimensions in one comparable number, but depend on data quality and weighting choices, and national averages can hide inequality between regions, classes and ethnic groups. items.stem:
Source A
The Gender Inequality Index shows that no country has achieved gender equality. Women are disadvantaged in reproductive health, hold fewer parliamentary seats and are less likely to participate in the labour market. The greatest inequality is found in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
— UNDP, Human Development Report (2023/24) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source A about measuring and addressing inequality. [3]
items.answer: reproductive health; parliamentary representation; labour market participation
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: reproductive health; parliamentary representation; labour market participation. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source B
Quotas are a fast track to equal representation. Where they have been well designed – with placement rules and sanctions for non-compliance – the share of women in parliament has risen sharply. Where they lack enforcement, they have little effect.
— International IDEA, Gender Quotas Database commentary (paraphrased)

With reference to Source B, explain why the source suggests that the design of quotas matters. [4]
items.answer: Without placement rules, parties can put women in unwinnable positions; without sanctions, they can ignore quotas, so effective design determines whether quotas change outcomes.
items.markingKey: Without placement rules, parties can put women in unwinnable positions; without sanctions, they can ignore quotas, so effective design determines whether quotas change outcomes. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Affirmative action does more to entrench group identities than to reduce inequality."
items.answer: Affirmative action has reduced some inequalities, though its design must avoid benefiting only elites within groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reinforces caste and racial categories; benefits may go to better-off members (“creamy layer”); backlash (SFFA v Harvard). Arguments against: increased representation of excluded groups in India and the USA; addresses structural discrimination; colour-blind policies can preserve inequality. Supported judgement: Affirmative action has reduced some inequalities, though its design must avoid benefiting only elites within groups.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Gender Inequality Index (GII)"?

items.stem: A student claims: "Gender quotas guarantee that women in parliament have real power." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Quotas increase numbers but women may be excluded from senior positions or controlled by party leaders; Rwanda has a female majority in parliament within a dominant-party system.

items.stem: An IPU-style dataset shows that 10 of the 60 members of the lower house of Country G (an Andean state) are women. (a) Calculate the percentage of seats held by women. (b) A proposed reserved-seat quota requires that at least 40% of seats be held by women. Calculate the minimum number of additional women needed to meet it, assuming the size of the assembly is unchanged. [3]
items.answer: (a) 10/60 = 16.7%; (b) 40% of 60 = 24 → at least 24 women needed, so 14 more
items.markingKey: A1 16.7%; M1 40/100 × 60 = 24; A1 14 additional women.

items.stem: Briefly describe the end of race-conscious admissions in the USA (2023) and explain what it reveals about contestation over affirmative action.
items.answer: The Supreme Court ruled against Harvard and the University of North Carolina, ending most race-based affirmative action in admissions. The ruling reflects the view that equal treatment requires colour-blind policies, opposed by those who argue substantive equality requires positive measures.
items.markingKey: Context (The Supreme Court ruled against Harvard and the University of North Carolina, ending most race-based affirmative action in admissions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. The principle that all citizens have equal rights to participate in and influence political decisions, summarised as “one person, one vote”

items.stem: Using South Africa after apartheid as an example, explain the gap between political and economic equality.
